near_miss.lead: Bright day: lios dagr; ahar ... śukraṃ
near_miss.why_not: The Norse nominative adjective describes ordinary morning; the Vedic words describe the generation of luminous day. Neither day nor bright is an exact cognate pair here. Wider searches for bright/day found AVŚ 4,1.s10, another version of the Vedic passage, but no diagnostic Norse–Indic formula. The Irish mouse passages paired with bundle 14 have no corresponding expression.

near_miss.lead: Possessing cattle or wealth: fe beside paśūnām
near_miss.why_not: The Norse treasure is gold, silver and valuables formerly owned by Gunnar. Indic divine lordship over terrestrial animals differs in predicate, syntax and context. The semantic history of fé is real, but the shared noun is not evidence of an inherited phrase.

near_miss.lead: Battle dead feed wolf and raven: ulfs beitu; hrafn né svalta
near_miss.why_not: This is recognizable Germanic battle imagery, but its slab partner concerns a ritual hide and protection of a married couple. Searches of Rigvedic, Atharvavedic and epic wolf expressions returned predators, pastoral threats, animal similes and a personal name, not a matching carrion-feeding collocation. The initial root/lemma conjunction returned no hits; that alone was not treated as absence.

near_miss.lead: Eating food and drinking water: æta byg; drecka vatn
near_miss.why_not: Norse eta and the Hittite eating verb are cognate; vatn and wātar are cognate, with distinct drinking verbs. But starvation in a treasure chamber and routine horse feeding/watering provide only an everyday conjunction of eating and drinking. The Atharvavedic food-eating passage supplies no distinctive parallel. No inherited poetic or ritual formula is justified.

near_miss.lead: Slaying the serpent: vá orminn; killing worms
near_miss.why_not: Norse ormr and Sanskrit krimi can be compared etymologically, but Sigurðr killing a dragon and an anti-worm charm are different settings. The Norse slaying verb does not supply the Indic han cognate. Searches found the same Norse episode in DG-8-OHleg 0057:28 (w6/12), an unrelated hook striking a serpent, a personal-name false hit, and Atharvavedic worm-killing spells; none repairs the missing cross-branch phrase. The general dragon-slaying comparison was recalled, not a newly established equation.

near_miss.lead: Bound in bonds: bǫndum / bundit; badhyate bandhe; bandhena baddho
near_miss.why_not: All preserve the bind root, but Norse has sitting in bonds followed by a separate passive clause, not the Sanskrit cognate noun governed by the binding verb. Corpus searches show productive applications to marriage (AVŚ 14,1.s52), loads (MBh 1,213.s104), fettered feet (MBh 8,37.s48) and yogic restraint (MBh 12,308.s36; 13,41.s24). Captivity, erotic subjection and dharmic obligation do not establish a distinctive inherited construction.

Norse sofa, Greek hypnos and Sanskrit sup- preserve the sleep root, and Norse nótt is cognate with Greek nyx. Yet normal sleeping at night, sleepless heroic nights, sleep seizing Achilles and a nocturnal arrival use different predicates and syntax. Ordinary narrative circumstances suffice to explain the overlap.

near_miss.lead: Wind and sail: vinda rift; uela ... uentus
near_miss.why_not: Wind is cognate, but the Norse genitive kenning names the sail as cloth of winds; Latin has wind propelling a ship and its sails in a physical analogy. The nouns for sail are not an established cognate pair and the syntactic figure differs.

near_miss.lead: Green vegetation: grǿnna lyngva; зеленой лугъ
near_miss.why_not: The Norse expression occurs in compressed skaldic serpent/treasure imagery, whereas the byliny describe people assembling on a meadow. Lyng and Slavic lug must not be equated from superficial similarity or the automatic mapping; no shared syntactic figure is established. The Fáfnismál witness is within Germanic and cannot anchor a cross-branch claim.

near_miss.lead: Brothers covet or withhold cattle/wealth: brœðr ... fe; bhrātṛbhyāṃ paśu-lubdhābhyām
near_miss.why_not: Brother and cattle/wealth are exact cognates and both stories involve selfish relatives. But the Norse finite possession and refusal to share differ from a Sanskrit instrumental agent modified by a cattle-greedy compound. Kinship conflict over wealth is too general to demonstrate an inherited phrase, and the Sanskrit desire root has no matching Norse predicate.

The adjective and wind root are cognate, but great wind is a freely compositional weather expression. The Norse travellers encounter wind and rain; Sanskrit compares a fallen warrior to an ocean dried by a great wind mass. No distinctive common figure or context strengthens the lexical pair.

The Norse king lays hands on an afflicted side and sings prayers in a Christian miracle. Thetis strokes a grieving Achilles and asks why he cries. Neither the hand words nor the verbal formulas establish the required inherited collocation; the functional resemblance is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Warrior and dog simile: sem hunda; κύων ὥς
near_miss.why_not: The dog words are cognate, but Norse compares defeated men to beaten dogs, whereas Homer compares an attacker to a hound pursuing a fawn. Opposite roles and different predicates prevent treating the commonplace animal comparison as the same inherited figure.

Norse dag ok nótt expresses continuous riding; the Homeric juxtaposition of night and day concerns their paths, while Latin specifies yesterday and an arrival during this night. The day terms differ etymologically and the temporal expressions are too ordinary to reconstruct a formula.

The Norse adjective and noun form a transparent cognate construction in the context-before line. The Greek partner concerns surrendering Helen to avert losses and has no corresponding wound expression. The Norse internal figure alone cannot supply a cross-branch claim.

The Norse sword sings against helmets; the Greek partner concerns hearing a human voice. The sound image is potentially poetic, but no cognate weapon-and-song collocation occurs in the supplied comparison.

near_miss.lead: Anger produces fire from the mouth
near_miss.why_not: The Norse supernatural fire burns an opponent through his armour. The supplied partners concern cultivation, accepting advice and salt at a river mouth. The mouth overlap is anatomical versus geographical, and none supplies an inherited anger/fire phrase.

error.correct_reading: svelta, starve/die of hunger; preterite form based on svalt, not svala, cool.
error.evidence: The subject is hrafn, and the negated predicate says that the raven did not starve amid the battle dead. The neighbouring wolf-food image confirms the sense.

error.correct_reading: Genitive singular of ulfr, wolf; inherited *wĺ̥kʷos (compare Sanskrit vṛka).
error.evidence: The genitive modifies beitu in the wolf-food image. Unmapped omits a secure inherited animal noun.

error.correct_reading: Preterite singular of vega, slay/fight. Remove the transporting *weǵʰ- alternative in this context; the supplied overcome alternative is the relevant comparison.
error.evidence: Sigurðr is the subject and the dragon is the object; the depicted event is killing, not transport.

error.correct_reading: hræðiligr, comparative hræðiligri, more terrifying (predicative masculine singular).
error.evidence: The surface form retains initial hræði- and is coordinated with mæiri in the dragon description; ræðiligr drops the initial h and misidentifies the stem.

error.correct_reading: Ormr (personal name), genitive singular; exclude from common-noun worm matches.
error.evidence: Orms modifies lík and is followed by konungsbróður, identifying the corpse of the king’s brother, subsequently transported and buried.

error.correct_reading: hann, nominative singular pronoun referring to Eckinvarðr.
error.evidence: The temporal clause requires the subject of kemr; intrusive r in hrann gives no appropriate word. This reports the evident text corruption without claiming to identify its production stage.

given_etymon.gloss: to desire, covet, want (someone or something); to admire, praise; to love; to be disturbed

error.correct_reading: lubh, covet/desire, instrumental dual participle qualifying the brothers; remove the cut-off *lewbʰ- alternative.
error.evidence: The compound paśu-lubdhābhyām means greedy for cattle; a cutting root does not explain the construction.
